docs.title: Philter SDK for Java
docs.text:
The Philter SDK for Java is an API client for Philter. Philter identifies and manipulates sensitive information such as Protected Health Information (PHI) and personally identifiable information (PII) in natural language text. Philter is built upon the open source PII/PHI detection engine Phileas.

Refer to the Philter API specification for details on the available endpoints.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Releases are available from Maven Central. Add the dependency to your Maven configuration:

<dependency>
    <groupId>ai.philterd</groupId>
    <artifactId>philter-sdk-java</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0</version>
</dependency>

To track the latest development build, depend on the current -SNAPSHOT version and add the Maven Central snapshot repository to your build (snapshots are not served from the default Maven Central repository):

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>central-portal-snapshots</id>
        <url>https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/</url>
        <releases>
            <enabled>false</enabled>
        </releases>
        <snapshots>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </snapshots>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependency>
    <groupId>ai.philterd</groupId>
    <artifactId>philter-sdk-java</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

Snapshots are development builds: they are mutable and are periodically pruned, so pin a release version for anything you need to reproduce.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
As of version 3.0.0, this client targets the Philter 4.0.0 API. Earlier versions of the client are not compatible with Philter 4.0.0 and later.

philter-sdk-java Philter API Branch 3.0.0 and later 4.x main 2.0.0 none (do not use) 1.x 1.x to 3.x 1.x

Development for Philter 4.x happens on the main branch. The 1.x branch supports Philter 3 and earlier.

The 2.0.0 on Maven Central was published in June 2026 against an early Philter 4.0 API that has since changed, so it does not work with Philter 4.0.0. Use 3.0.0 or later.

The client requires Java 11 or later. Requests are made with the JDK's java.net.http.HttpClient, so the SDK adds no third-party HTTP dependency to your application.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
With an available running instance of Philter, to filter text:

import ai.philterd.philter.PhilterClient;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.FilterResponse;

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://127.0.0.1:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .build();

FilterResponse filterResponse = client.filter("context", "default", text);

To filter text with explanation:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ExplainResponse;

ExplainResponse explainResponse = client.explain("context", "default", text);

Philter 4.0.0 expects an Authorization header on nearly every endpoint. Provide its value with withApiKey(...); the value is sent verbatim, so include any scheme prefix (for example "Bearer ") if your deployment requires it. The health() endpoint does not require authentication.

In addition to filtering, the client covers the full Philter 4.0.0 API: policies (including versions, diffs, rollbacks, descriptions and notes, managed policies, and copies), contexts, documents, legal holds, the redaction ledger, the audit log and its CSV export, custom lists, redact lists, re-identification, user management, sign-in with passwords, session keys, and MFA, webhooks, managing API keys, rotating the output signing key, admin settings, and administrator listings of policies, contexts, custom lists, ledger chains, and legal holds across all users. Every endpoint in the API specification has a corresponding method, and every optional query parameter can be supplied.

docs.title: Admin Settings
docs.text:
The admin settings apply to the whole deployment: differential-privacy count recording, output signing, the webhook destination allowlist, and Phield publishing. Reading them requires the settings:read scope, and changing them settings:write. Both also require an administrator.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.AdminSettings;

AdminSettings settings = client.getAdminSettings();

settings.isDiffuseCountsEnabled();   // record PII counts for differential-privacy reporting
settings.isSigningEnabled();         // sign every text filter and explain response
settings.getWebhookAllowlist();      // where webhooks may point; empty allows any public address
settings.isPhieldEnabled();
settings.getPhieldUrl();
settings.getPhieldSourceId();
settings.getPhieldOrganization();
settings.isPhieldApiKeySet();        // the key itself is never returned
settings.isMfaAvailable();           // users may enroll in MFA for sign-in
settings.isMfaRequired();            // every user who signs in must enroll

// Read-only: set by the deployment's environment, not by updateAdminSettings.
settings.isCrossUserAccessEnabled();     // ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED
settings.isLedgerDeletionEnabled();      // LEDGER_DELETION_ENABLED
settings.isSigningKeyExternallyManaged(); // PHILTER_SIGNING_KEY_PATH: the key cannot be rotated over the API

docs.title: Changing settings
docs.text:
Set only the settings to change. The rest are not sent, and Philter leaves them as they are.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.UpdateAdminSettingsRequest;

UpdateAdminSettingsRequest request = new UpdateAdminSettingsRequest();
request.setSigningEnabled(true);
request.setWebhookAllowlist("hooks.example.com, 10.4.0.0/16");

AdminSettings saved = client.updateAdminSettings(request);

for (String warning : saved.getWarnings()) {
    System.out.println(warning);
}
  • webhookAllowlist is comma-separated hostnames, IP addresses, and CIDR ranges. An empty string allows any public address.
  • phieldApiKey sets the Phield API key. An empty string removes it.
  • phieldSourceId and phieldOrganization are set to philter when blank.
  • mfaRequired requires mfaAvailable; turning it on while mfaAvailable is off is an HTTP 400. Users already enrolled in MFA are asked for a code whatever mfaAvailable says. See Multi-factor authentication.

Philter validates every value before saving any, and changes nothing if one is invalid. A webhookAllowlist entry that is not a hostname, an IP address, or a CIDR range, a phieldUrl that is not an absolute http or https URL, or a request that sets phieldEnabled or phieldUrl and would leave Phield enabled without a URL is an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException carrying Philter's reason.

An http Phield URL with an API key is saved, and getWarnings() on the response says the key will be sent in the clear. It is empty on a read.

Each Philter instance caches the settings for up to ADMIN_SETTINGS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS. A change applies at once on the instance that made it, and on other instances when their cache expires.

A change is recorded in Philter's audit log as a settings_updated event naming the settings that changed. Their values are not recorded.

docs.title: Audit Log
docs.text: Philter records security-relevant actions and redaction activity in its audit log. getAuditLog reads it as typed events, and exportAuditLog exports it as CSV for a range of whole days. Both require the audit:read scope and an administrator, and each read or export is itself recorded in the log.

docs.title: Reading the audit log
docs.text:
import ai.philterd.philter.model.AuditEvent;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetAuditLogResponse;
import java.time.Instant;

// The most recent events, unfiltered.
GetAuditLogResponse recent = client.getAuditLog();

// Policy deletions in September 2026, 100 at a time.
GetAuditLogResponse page = client.getAuditLog("policy_deleted",
        Instant.parse("2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"), Instant.parse("2026-10-01T00:00:00Z"), null, 0, 100);

long total = page.getTotal();
for (AuditEvent e : page.getEvents()) {
    // The actor's username, or null when the actor is not a user.
    System.out.println(e.getTimestamp() + " " + e.getEvent() + " by " + e.getUsername() + ": " + e.getDetails());
}

Events are returned most recent first. Every filter may be null:

  • event - one event type, such as policy_deleted. A name Philter does not record is an HTTP 400 rather than an empty page.
  • from and to - from is inclusive and to exclusive, so a day's events are from that day to the next.
  • owner - the username of the acting user. Your own username always works; another user's requires ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED=true, and a username that does not exist is an HTTP 404. Some events record the affected entity rather than the acting user, so an owner filter does not return them.
  • offset and limit - page through the matches (default 25, at most 100). getTotal() is the number of events matching the filters.

Every field of an AuditEvent except getTimestamp() and getEvent() is null for an event that did not record it. Audit events never carry redacted values.

getApiKeyId() is the id of the acting principal. Despite its name, for most events it is the id of the user who acted, the same id as User.getId(), and getUsername() is that user's username, even for a user since deactivated. For some events the principal is something else, such as a policy, a list, or an API key; getUsername() is then null, as it is for an event with no user actor and for events from a Philter without philterd/philter#161. The CSV export has no username column; its api_key_id column holds the same id.

getSource() says where an event came from: api for an event a request caused, including a redaction the asynchronous worker completes later, or system for one Philter recorded on its own, such as at startup or when a session key expires in the background. getClientIpAddress() is the address of the client whose request caused the event (the connection's address or, for a request from a trusted proxy, the address its X-Forwarded-For names), and null for an event with no request behind it. Events recorded by a Philter without philterd/philter#149 have no source, and some hold api or system in the client address instead. For the list of event types and what each field holds, see Philter's auditing documentation.

docs.title: Exporting as CSV
docs.text:
exportAuditLog returns the log as CSV for a range of whole days.

// October 1 through 5, both days included, read in UTC.
AuditLogExport export = client.exportAuditLog(
        LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 5), ZoneId.of("UTC"), null, null);

String csv = export.getCsv();          // or getContent() for the bytes
int rows = export.getRows();

The CSV has a header row and the columns timestamp, event, request_id, api_key_id, associated_object, client_ip_address, source, and details, the same fields as an AuditEvent except its getUsername(). A Philter without philterd/philter#149 has no source column.

from and to are read in the given time zone, or in the Philter server's time zone when it is null or omitted. getTimeZone() reports the zone Philter used. Timestamps in the CSV are UTC whatever the zone. A range may span at most 31 days (to at most 30 days after from).

docs.title: Paging
docs.text:
An export returns one page, most recent first: up to limit events (default 100, at most 1000). When isTruncated() is true, more events remain. Page through with exportAuditLogAfter, passing each page's getNextCursor() to get the next, and null for the first:

ZoneId utc = ZoneId.of("UTC");
LocalDate to = LocalDate.now(utc);            // a range that includes today
LocalDate from = to.minusDays(7);             // at most 30 days before to

String cursor = null;
do {
    AuditLogExport page = client.exportAuditLogAfter(from, to, utc, cursor, 1000);
    // write page.getContent()
    cursor = page.isTruncated() ? page.getNextCursor() : null;
} while (cursor != null);

A cursor marks the last event of its page, and the next page holds the events after it. Events recorded while you page, including the audit_log_exported event each page records, are newer than the cursor, so they never move events between pages: paging by cursor returns each event in the range exactly once, even when the range includes the current day. Events recorded after the first page are normally left out; export again to include them. Keep from, to, and the zone the same on every page. A cursor that is not one from an export page is an HTTP 400 whose getField() is cursor.

Every page starts with the CSV header row, so drop it from each page after the first when concatenating.

Paging with exportAuditLog(from, to, zone, offset, limit) and getNextOffset() still works, and returns each event once for a range of past days. For a range that includes the current day it can repeat events across pages, because each page's own export, and any other activity, is recorded as a new event that moves older ones onto later pages; use the cursor for such a range. A page read by cursor has no next offset, and a page read by offset has both.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Philter rejects a reversed range, a range longer than 31 days, or an unknown time zone with an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException whose message carries Philter's reason. A caller who is not an administrator gets an HTTP 403, also as a ClientException. See Error Handling.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Policy: A named set of rules that tells Philter which entity types to find (names, SSNs, email addresses, dates, and so on) and what filter strategy to apply to each (redact, replace, mask, encrypt, hash, and others). Every filter request names the policy to apply; Philter ships a policy named default. Policies are authored as JSON; this client treats the policy body as an opaque JSON string.
  • Context: An arbitrary label used to group requests (for example, by tenant or job). It is passed on each filter request and is echoed back on the response.
  • Document ID: Philter assigns an identifier to each filtered document and returns it in the X-Document-Id response header; the client exposes it on the response object.
  • Consistent pseudonymization: Replacing a value with a stand-in, and using the same stand-in for that value everywhere. Philter records the mapping as entries on the context, so the property holds across documents and requests that share a context. This is what preserves referential integrity: relationships and joins in the redacted output still line up, because one source value has exactly one replacement.
  • Re-identification: The CRYPTO_REPLACE and FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE strategies are reversible, value by value, through reidentifyValues(...). reidentifyText(...) restores every CRYPTO_REPLACE value in a text, such as an LLM's response to a redacted prompt. Redaction, masking, and hashing are not reversible. See Re-identification.

docs.title: Contexts
docs.text:
Contexts group related requests under an arbitrary label and can enable features such as entity-type disambiguation and the redaction ledger.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.DisambiguationScope;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GenericResponse;

// Create a context with entity-type disambiguation and the ledger enabled.
GenericResponse created = client.createContext("tenant-a", true, true);

// Or have disambiguation learn across every document redacted in the context.
client.createContext("tenant-b", true, DisambiguationScope.CONTEXT, true, null);

// Then pass the context name on filter/explain calls.
client.filter("tenant-a", "default", "Some text...");

// Update or delete the context.
client.updateContext("tenant-a", false, true);
client.updateContext("tenant-a", null, DisambiguationScope.CONTEXT, null, null);
client.deleteContext("tenant-a");

A user can have at most 10 contexts, counting default. createContext is refused with a 409, raised as a ClientException, whose getReason() is context_limit_reached at the limit and context_exists for a name the user already has. See Error Handling.

A context name is used in request paths, so it cannot contain /, \, ;, %, or a control character, and cannot be . or ..; Philter refuses one that does with an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException. Since no context can have such a name, deleteContext always names the context in the path.

On createContext, a setting passed as null takes its default: false for both flags, and document for the disambiguation scope. On updateContext, only the settings given change; one passed as null keeps its current value. An update that gives no setting is refused with a 400.

The disambiguation scope sets what span disambiguation learns from when entity-type disambiguation is enabled:

  • DisambiguationScope.DOCUMENT (document, the default): each document is disambiguated on its own, from what Philter learns in that document. Nothing is stored.
  • DisambiguationScope.CONTEXT (context): what Philter learns is stored and used for every later document redacted in the context. It is kept if the scope or disambiguation changes, and deleted when the context is emptied or deleted.

The value is not case-sensitive. Any other value is refused with a 400, raised as a ClientException, and an update refused this way changes no setting.

List the contexts, and inspect or clear the values a context has accumulated:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ContextDetails;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ContextSummary;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ContextEntriesExport;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ImportContextEntriesResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ContextEntry;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetContextEntriesResponse;

// The first page of contexts, each with its name and when it was created.
List<ContextSummary> contexts = client.listContexts().getContexts();

// The context's settings and its entries counted by filter type.
ContextDetails context = client.getContextDetails("tenant-a");
long size = context.getSize();
Map<String, Long> byFilterType = context.getFilterTypes();
String scope = context.getDisambiguationScope();

// Its entries, a page at a time. The original values are never returned.
GetContextEntriesResponse page = client.listContextEntries("tenant-a", null, 0, 100);
for (ContextEntry entry : page.getEntries()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getFilterType() + " -> " + entry.getReplacement());
}

// Its mapping table, to load into another context.
ContextEntriesExport export = client.getContextEntriesExport("tenant-a");
ImportContextEntriesResponse imported = client.importContextEntriesExport("tenant-b", export);

client.deleteContextEntry("tenant-a", entryId);
client.deleteContextEntries("tenant-a");

getContextDetails returns the context's settings (isEntityTypeDisambiguation(), getDisambiguationScope(), which is document or context, and isLedger()), its size, and its entries counted by filter type. The counts are computed by Philter in one query and sum to size; untyped counts entries with no filter type, which only an import creates.

{
  "size": 125,
  "filterTypes": {
    "EMAIL_ADDRESS": 40,
    "PERSON": 83
  },
  "untyped": 2,
  "entityTypeDisambiguation": true,
  "disambiguationScope": "document",
  "ledger": false
}

A context's entries are its token-to-replacement mapping table, which is what gives consistent pseudonymization its referential integrity: the same source value keeps the same replacement until the entries are deleted. An export carries only token hashes and their replacements, never the original values, so it can be moved between environments: the hash is a plain SHA-256 of the value, the same on every Philter.

getContextEntriesExport returns the export as a ContextEntriesExport, and importContextEntriesExport(name, export, onConflict, owner) loads it into a context, here or on another Philter, with no JSON to handle. For a value the context already has, onConflict skip (the default) keeps the existing replacement and overwrite replaces it. The result says how many entries were getInserted(), getOverwritten(), and getSkipped(), out of getTotal(). Philter checks every entry before writing any, so a malformed export imports nothing.

docs.title: Creating a Client
docs.text:
Clients are created with the PhilterClientBuilder. Only the endpoint is required. Philter 4.0.0 expects an Authorization header on nearly every endpoint, so supply your API key with withApiKey(...). The value is sent verbatim, so include any scheme prefix (for example "Bearer ") if your deployment requires it.

import ai.philterd.philter.PhilterClient;

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .build();

A PhilterClient is thread-safe and reusable, so create one and share it for the lifetime of your application. The timeout can be set on the builder:

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .withTimeout(60)                 // connect and per-request timeout, seconds
        .build();

Requests are made with the JDK's java.net.http.HttpClient, so the SDK adds no third-party HTTP dependency to your application.

For full control over the HTTP stack (proxies, a custom executor, and so on) supply your own HttpClient.Builder. The connect timeout is then yours to configure; the per-request timeout, the Authorization header, and the client address are still applied. The TLS options below configure the SDK's own HTTP client, so they cannot be combined with your own builder: configure TLS on it instead.

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.time.Duration;

HttpClient.Builder http = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60));
// ...configure TLS, proxy, executor, etc...

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .withHttpClientBuilder(http)
        .build();

Connection pooling is tuned with the JDK's own system properties (jdk.httpclient.connectionPoolSize, jdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout) rather than on the builder.

docs.title: TLS and client certificates
docs.text:
By default the client trusts the server certificates the JVM trusts and presents no client certificate. Three builder options change that, without giving up the SDK's other defaults such as the connect timeout:

  • withClientCertificate(Path keyStore, char[] password) presents a client certificate for mutual TLS, from a PKCS12 or JKS keystore holding the certificate and its private key. Use it when Philter sits behind a load balancer, ingress, or service mesh that requires client certificates.
  • withTrustStore(Path trustStore, char[] password) trusts the certificates in a PKCS12 or JKS trust store instead of the JVM's defaults. Use it when the server's certificate comes from a private certificate authority or is self-signed, such as the certificate the Philter Docker image generates.
  • withSslContext(SSLContext) uses an SSLContext you build, for anything the other two do not cover, such as a key in a hardware module or certificates loaded from PEM files.
import java.nio.file.Path;

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://philter.internal.example.com:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .withClientCertificate(Path.of("/etc/philter-client/client.p12"), keyStorePassword)
        .withTrustStore(Path.of("/etc/philter-client/ca.p12"), trustStorePassword)
        .build();

Either keystore option can be used alone: a client certificate with the JVM's default trust, or a trust store without a client certificate. The format of each file is detected from its contents. A client certificate's private key must use the keystore's password, as it does in a PKCS12 file. Passwords are copied, so you may clear your arrays once the builder has them.

The files are read when build() is called. A file that is missing, cannot be read with its password, or holds nothing usable (no private key in a client certificate keystore, no trusted certificates in a trust store) is refused with an IllegalArgumentException that names the file and never the password. Combining withSslContext with either keystore option, or any of the three with withHttpClientBuilder, is refused with an IllegalStateException.

Hostname verification stays on with every option: the server's certificate must name the host in the endpoint. If the server asks for a client certificate and the client has none it accepts, the call fails with an IOException.

To build a PKCS12 keystore from PEM files, for example ones issued by cert-manager or a service mesh:

openssl pkcs12 -export -in client.crt -inkey client.key -out client.p12
keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ca -file ca.crt -keystore ca.p12 -storetype PKCS12 -storepass <password>

Build the trust store with keytool -importcert as shown. A PKCS12 trust store made with openssl pkcs12 -export -nokeys reads as empty in Java, because its certificates lack the attribute Java uses to mark trusted certificates, and build() refuses it.

docs.title: With your own HTTP client builder
docs.text:
The TLS options above cannot be combined with withHttpClientBuilder, since your builder carries its own TLS settings. To use the same keystores with your own builder, build the SSLContext with PhilterTls.sslContext and set it on your builder:

import ai.philterd.philter.PhilterTls;
import javax.net.ssl.SSLContext;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.time.Duration;

SSLContext context = PhilterTls.sslContext(
        Path.of("/etc/philter-client/client.p12"), keyStorePassword,
        Path.of("/etc/philter-client/ca.p12"), trustStorePassword);

HttpClient.Builder http = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
        .sslContext(context);

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://philter.internal.example.com:8080")
        .withApiKey("your-api-key")
        .withHttpClientBuilder(http)
        .build();

Your builder gets none of the SDK's HTTP client defaults, so set a connect timeout on it as shown: the JDK's builder has none, and follows no redirects unless told to.

PhilterTls.sslContext reads the files the same way withClientCertificate and withTrustStore do, and refuses an unusable file with the same IllegalArgumentException. Either store may be null, but not both: with no keystore no client certificate is presented, and with no trust store the JVM's default trust applies. The files are read when it is called, so build the context once and share it across clients.

docs.title: Requests on behalf of a person
docs.text:
An application that calls Philter for the people using it, such as a web front end, can pass each person's address with withClientAddress. It is sent as X-Forwarded-For on every request, so wherever Philter records a request's client address, such as on audit events and for the sign-in rate limit, it records the person's address rather than the application's:

PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
        .withApiKey("Bearer " + sessionKey)
        .withClientAddress(() -> person.getAddress())
        .build();

The supplier is called for each request, on the thread making it, so an address that changes during a session is sent from the next request, and a client shared across people can return the address of the person whose request is being handled. A null result, an empty string, or only spaces sends no header. A result containing a comma, a control character such as a line break, a character outside ASCII, or a space within it is refused with an IllegalArgumentException before the request is sent.

Philter uses the header only when the request comes from an address in its TRUSTED_PROXIES, which by default is loopback only, so unless the application runs on the same host as Philter, list the application's address there; otherwise, and for a value that is not an IP address, it uses the address of the connection. A port is allowed and ignored. Return an address the application determined itself, such as the remote address of the person's connection to it, not one the person's browser supplied, which they can set to anything.

docs.title: Custom Lists
docs.text:
Custom lists let a policy match (or ignore) an explicit set of terms.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.CustomListSummary;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.CustomList;
import java.util.List;

// Create a list of terms. A name already in use is refused.
client.saveList("blocked-terms", "Terms to always redact", List.of("Acme", "Project X"));

// Replace the list's terms. A null description keeps the current one; "" clears it.
client.replaceList("blocked-terms", null, List.of("Acme", "Project X", "Project Y"));

// Retrieve a list's items and description.
CustomList list = client.getList("blocked-terms");
System.out.println(list.getItems() + " " + list.getDescription());

// A page of lists, with each one's name, description, and size but not its terms, and the total.
Page<CustomListSummary> lists = client.listCustomLists(null, new ListOptions().search("blocked"));
for (CustomListSummary summary : lists.getItems()) {
    System.out.println(summary.getName() + " (" + summary.getSize() + ")");
}

// Delete a list.
client.deleteList("blocked-terms");

saveList only creates. A name the owner already uses is refused with a ClientException whose getStatusCode() is 409 and getReason() is list_exists; replace the list with replaceList instead, which is refused with a 404 if there is no such list. A list holds up to 100 items of up to 50 characters each, and a description of up to 200 characters; more is an HTTP 400. getLimits().getCustomLists() reports these limits.

A list name is used in request paths, so it cannot contain /, \, ;, %, or a control character, and cannot be . or ... saveList with such a name gets an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException whose getReason() is invalid_request. Since no list can have such a name, deleteList always names the list in the path.

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text:
import ai.philterd.philter.PhilterClient;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ExplainResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.FilterResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.Span;

public class RedactionExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        PhilterClient client = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
                .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
                .withApiKey("your-api-key")
                .build();

        final String text = "Patient George Washington (SSN 123-45-6789) was seen on 03/14.";

        // 1. Redact.
        FilterResponse filtered = client.filter("clinic", "default", text);
        System.out.println("Redacted: " + filtered.getFilteredText());
        System.out.println("Document ID: " + filtered.getDocumentId());

        // 2. Explain what was found.
        ExplainResponse explained = client.explain("clinic", "default", text);
        for (Span span : explained.getExplanation().getAppliedSpans()) {
            System.out.printf("  %-12s %-20s -> %s%n",
                    span.getFilterType(), span.getText(), span.getReplacement());
        }
    }

}

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Every operation declares a checked IOException, thrown when the request cannot be executed (network failure, timeout, and so on). In addition, non-successful HTTP responses are mapped to unchecked exceptions:

HTTP status Exception 401 UnauthorizedException 429 from signIn or completeSignIn SignInLockedException or SignInRateLimitedException 503 ServiceUnavailableException any other non-2xx ClientException

Philter explains a rejected request in the response body, and the ClientException message carries it (truncated at 512 characters) after the status code, so a 400 or a 403 says what was actually wrong:

Unknown error: HTTP 400: {"message":"'strategy' must be CRYPTO_REPLACE or FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE."}

UnauthorizedException and ServiceUnavailableException carry what ClientException does: getStatusCode() (401 or 503), getErrorMessage(), getReason(), and getRequestId(). Their message is Philter's message, or Unauthorized or Service unavailable when the response has none, followed by the request id when the response has one; getErrorMessage() and getReason() are then null.

A 401's getReason() tells apart why the credentials were refused, so a user interface can, for example, send a person whose session ended back to sign in:

getReason() Meaning invalid_credentials The key is missing, malformed, or unknown, or is a revoked long-lived key. session_expired The session key expired, was revoked, or signed out. Sign in again. user_deactivated The key's user is deactivated. 
try {
    client.listPolicies(null, null);
} catch (UnauthorizedException e) {
    if (ErrorReasons.SESSION_EXPIRED.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // Show the sign-in page.
    }
}

Neither is a subclass of ClientException, so a catch (ClientException e) does not catch a 401 or a 503, and a multi-catch of ClientException | ServiceUnavailableException compiles. All three implement PhilterError, which has the four accessors, to handle any Philter error the same way:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.PhilterError;

try {
    client.listPolicies(null, null);
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    if (e instanceof PhilterError) {
        PhilterError error = (PhilterError) e;
        log.warn("Philter refused the request: {} {} ({}, request id {})", error.getStatusCode(),
                error.getErrorMessage(), error.getReason(), error.getRequestId());
    }
    throw e;
}

SignInLockedException and SignInRateLimitedException are subclasses of ClientException, so a handler for ClientException still catches them. See Failed sign-ins.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.FilterResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ServiceUnavailableException;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.UnauthorizedException;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ClientException;
import java.io.IOException;

try {
    FilterResponse response = client.filter("my-context", "default", "Some text...");
    System.out.println(response.getFilteredText());
} catch (UnauthorizedException e) {
    // Bad or missing API key.
} catch (ServiceUnavailableException e) {
    // Philter is temporarily unavailable; consider retrying with backoff.
} catch (ClientException e) {
    // Other non-successful response.
} catch (IOException e) {
    // The request could not be completed.
}

docs.title: Acting on the reason
docs.text:
Every error Philter returns is a JSON object with a message, a reason, and, for some invalid requests, a field. ClientException exposes them as getErrorMessage(), getReason(), and getField(), alongside the HTTP status as getStatusCode().

  • getReason() is a stable, machine-readable code. Branch on it: it tells apart refusals that share a status, and it does not change when the wording does. ErrorReasons has a constant for every reason Philter gives. Philter gives one on every error: a specific reason where the refusal has one, and otherwise the one its status implies, such as ErrorReasons.NOT_FOUND for a 404.
  • getErrorMessage() is written for people, so show it rather than branching on it. It is read from the whole body, so it is complete even when the exception message was truncated.
  • getField() names the parameter or body field Philter found invalid, such as sort, password, or email, on some 400 responses whose reason is invalid_request, so a form can mark the field. It is null otherwise.

All three are null for a response that did not come from Philter, such as a proxy's error page; fall back to the status then. Compare with ErrorReasons.X.equals(e.getReason()), which is safe when the reason is null.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ErrorReasons;

try {
    client.changePassword(currentPassword, newPassword);
} catch (ClientException e) {
    if (ErrorReasons.WRONG_PASSWORD.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // The current password is not correct.
    } else if (ErrorReasons.INVALID_REQUEST.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // The new password was rejected; show the person why.
        System.out.println(e.getErrorMessage());
    } else if (ErrorReasons.CHANGED_CONCURRENTLY.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // Another request changed the password first; try again.
    } else {
        // Such as missing_scope, or a 409 conflict for a user with no password yet, whose first one an
        // administrator sets.
        throw e;
    }
}

The reasons for each call's own refusals are below; ErrorReasons documents every reason, including the general ones such as missing_scope, admin_required, session_expired, and not_found, and Philter's Errors documentation lists them with their statuses.

Call Status getReason() createContext 409 context_exists: the caller already has a context with that name, even at the limit. context_limit_reached: the caller already has the most contexts a user may have. savePolicy 409 policy_exists: the owner already has a policy with that name. Replace it with replacePolicy. replacePolicy 409 policy_managed: a managed policy cannot be replaced; copy it with copyPolicy and change the copy. policy_changed: the policy changed since the read whose entity tag you passed, or while the request was writing; read it again and retry. deletePolicy 409 policy_default: the default policy cannot be deleted. policy_managed: a managed policy cannot be deleted. copyPolicy 409 policy_exists: the owner already has a policy with the new name. rollbackPolicy 409 policy_managed: a managed policy cannot be rolled back. policy_changed: the policy changed since the read whose entity tag you passed, or while the request was writing; read it again and retry. setPolicyDetails 409 policy_managed: a managed policy's description and notes cannot be changed. policy_changed: the policy changed since the read whose entity tag you passed, or while the request was writing; read it again and retry. saveList 409 list_exists: the owner already has a list with that name. Replace it with replaceList. createHold 409 hold_exists: a hold with that reference exists. operation_in_progress: an evidence or hold operation for the owner is active or needs recovery. deleteHold 409 operation_in_progress, as for createHold. replaceRedactList 409 redact_list_changed: the list changed after the revision you passed. Read it again and retry. testWebhook 409 webhook_not_set: no webhook is set. getLedgerExport 422 entry_unreadable: an entry in the chain could not be read, so the chain is not exported. signIn 429 locked: the username is locked after repeated failures. rate_limited: the client address is over the sign-in rate limit. These are raised as SignInLockedException and SignInRateLimitedException. completeSignIn 429 rate_limited, raised as SignInRateLimitedException. The MFA step has no username lockout. 
try {
    client.createContext("tenant-a", false, false);
} catch (ClientException e) {
    if (ErrorReasons.CONTEXT_LIMIT_REACHED.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // Offer to delete a context first.
    } else if (ErrorReasons.CONTEXT_EXISTS.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // Choose another name.
    } else {
        throw e;
    }
}

getStatusCode() is 0 when the exception was not caused by a non-successful status, such as a response the client could not use. SignInLockedException and SignInRateLimitedException report 429.

docs.title: Request ids
docs.text:
Philter gives every API request an id and returns it in the X-Request-Id response header, on successes and refusals alike. It records the same id as request_id on every audit event the request causes, so the id ties what a client saw to what Philter recorded. Log it with errors, and quote it when asking an administrator, or Philterd support, about a request.

Every exception built from a Philter response carries it: ClientException (and so SignInLockedException and SignInRateLimitedException), UnauthorizedException, and ServiceUnavailableException all have getRequestId(), and their messages end with it, so a logged stack trace carries it without extra code:

Unknown error: HTTP 409: {"message":"A policy with this name already exists.","reason":"policy_exists"} (request id: 01929f2e-6c3a-7b1d-9e4f-3a2b1c0d9e8f)

getRequestId() is null when the response had none, as from a Philter version before 4.0, or when the exception was not caused by a response. getErrorMessage() is unchanged: it is Philter's message alone, without the id, for showing to people.

For a call that succeeded, getLastRequestId() returns the id of the most recent response the client received on the calling thread. Read it right after the call. It is kept per thread, so calls other threads make with the same client do not change it, and it is null when the thread's last call got no response, such as a connection failure.

try {
    client.replacePolicy("claims", policyJson);
    log.info("Replaced the claims policy (request id {})", client.getLastRequestId());
} catch (ClientException e) {
    log.warn("Philter refused the change: {} (request id {})", e.getErrorMessage(), e.getRequestId());
}

An administrator finds the request's audit events by their request_id, in the audit log's CSV export or with getAuditLog:

GetAuditLogResponse page = admin.getAuditLog(null, from, to, null, 0, 100);
page.getEvents().stream()
        .filter(event -> requestId.equals(event.getRequestId()))
        .forEach(event -> System.out.println(event.getEvent() + " " + event.getDetails()));

Redaction events are the exception: document_redaction_initiated and document_redaction_completed record the document id as their request_id, so a queued redaction's start and completion share one id. Find those by the document id, from FilterResponse.getDocumentId().

docs.title: Inspecting What Was Redacted (Explain)
docs.text:
When you need to know what Philter found and where, use explain(...). It returns the redacted text plus a structured explanation listing each span that was identified.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ExplainResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.Span;

ExplainResponse response = client.explain("my-context", "default",
        "His name is George Washington and his SSN is 123-45-6789.");

System.out.println("Redacted: " + response.getFilteredText());

for (Span span : response.getExplanation().getAppliedSpans()) {
    System.out.printf("Found %s \"%s\" at [%d, %d) -> replaced with \"%s\" (confidence %.2f)%n",
            span.getFilterType(),
            span.getText(),
            span.getCharacterStart(),
            span.getCharacterEnd(),
            span.getReplacement(),
            span.getConfidence());
}

getClassification() gives what a span was classified as beyond its filter type, and is null when the filter gives none. For a driver's license number it is the state whose format matched, such as UTAH; several states share a format, so treat it as a candidate rather than the issuing state. For a custom identifier or custom dictionary it is the classification set in the policy (custom-identifier by default for an identifier). PhEye spans have no classification.

Pass true as the last argument of explain(context, policyName, filename, text, sign) to ask for a signed response. getSignature() returns the signature, and getResponseBody() the JSON exactly as Philter sent it, which is what the signature covers. See Signed responses.

docs.title: Checking Server Health
docs.text:
health() does not require authentication and is useful for readiness checks.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.StatusResponse;

StatusResponse status = client.health();
System.out.println(status.getStatus());             // "UP" when Philter is healthy
System.out.println(status.getApplicationVersion()); // e.g. "4.0.0"
System.out.println(status.getRedactionPolicySchemaVersion());
System.out.println(status.getGitCommit());

getSigningKeyDetails() is also unauthenticated. It returns the public key that Philter signs its output with, as PEM and as a JWK, with its fingerprint, so a recipient can verify a signature without credentials. getSigningKeyDetails(keyId) returns a retained key by ID, for verifying output signed with a key that has since been rotated.

SigningKey key = client.getSigningKeyDetails();
String pem = key.getPem();

An administrator can rotate the signing key with regenerateSigningKey(), which requires the signing:write scope. Philter generates a new key and makes it active, and keeps the old one retrievable with getSigningKeyDetails(keyId), so output signed with it stays verifiable. Resolve each signature's key ID rather than caching one key. Where the key is managed by PHILTER_SIGNING_KEY_PATH, rotating over the API is refused with an HTTP 409; replace the file and restart every instance instead.

String activeKeyId = client.regenerateSigningKey();

docs.title: Redaction Ledger
docs.text:
The ledger records what Philter redacted, as a signed chain per document. Enable it on a context (see Contexts); it is off by default.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetLedgerResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.LedgerChain;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.LedgerExport;

// The head of each chain, most recent first, or of those whose document ID or filename matches.
GetLedgerResponse chains = client.listLedgerChains(null);
GetLedgerResponse matching = client.listLedgerChains("note.txt");
int total = chains.getTotal();

// The first page of one document's chain, and whether its hash chain and signatures verify.
LedgerChain chain = client.getLedgerChain(documentId);
boolean valid = chain.isValid();
Long entries = chain.getTotal();  // null if the chain could not be checked

// A later page: skip 25 entries and read up to 50.
LedgerChain next = client.getLedgerChain(documentId, null, 25, 50);

// Just whether it verifies, without the entries.
boolean stillValid = client.verifyLedgerChain(documentId).isValid();

// An export that verifies standalone. It carries the original redacted values.
LedgerExport export = client.getLedgerExport(documentId);

getLedgerChain returns a page of the chain, 25 entries unless a limit is given, and at most 100. The entries are in chain order, and getTotal() is how many the whole chain has, one per redacted span plus the genesis entry. isValid() and the other check results cover the whole chain, whichever page is read. getLedgerExport returns every entry at once.

A chain that is not valid either failed a check or could not be checked at all:

LedgerChain chain = client.verifyLedgerChain(documentId);
if (chain.isValid()) {
    // The hash chain and every signature verify.
} else if (chain.getValidationError() != null) {
    // Not checked, for example because an entry no longer decrypts. Not evidence of tampering.
    System.out.println(chain.getValidationError());
} else if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(chain.getHashChainValid())) {
    // An entry no longer matches its hash or its link to the previous entry.
} else {
    // chain.getSignaturesValid() is false: an entry is unsigned (counted by getUnsignedEntries())
    // or its signature does not verify.
}

When the chain could not be checked, getHashChainValid(), getSignaturesValid(), getSignedEntries(), getUnsignedEntries(), getEntries(), and getTotal() are null.

Reading or listing a chain does not return the values that were redacted, only their replacements. An export does, in each entry's getToken(), which is why it needs the ledger:export scope; treat it as sensitive.

An entry Philter can no longer read, for example because it no longer decrypts after a key change, is reported rather than failing the request. A chain whose head entry cannot be read is still listed by listLedgerChains and listLedgerChainsAcrossUsers, with LedgerEntry.getReadError() set and getReplacement() null; the fields stored in the clear, such as the document ID, filename, hashes, timestamp, and policy fields, are still given. getReadError() is null for an entry that was read. A listing shows only each chain's head, so a chain whose later entry cannot be read lists with no read error. A chain with any unreadable entry, head or later, is reported by getLedgerChain and verifyLedgerChain as one that could not be checked, and getLedgerExport refuses it, even in part, with a ClientException whose getStatusCode() is 422 and getReason() is entry_unreadable.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.LedgerEntry;

for (LedgerEntry head : client.listLedgerChains(null).getChains()) {
    if (head.getReadError() != null) {
        // Listed, but its replacement cannot be shown and the chain cannot be exported.
    }
}

listLedgerChains returns one page at a time. See Owners and Pagination to page through the rest, or to read another user's ledger as an administrator.

Verify an exported chain against the public signing key, which is served without authentication:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.SigningKey;

// The key an entry was signed with, by its getSigningKeyId(). Superseded keys stay retrievable.
SigningKey key = client.getSigningKeyDetails(entry.getSigningKeyId());
String pem = key.getPem();

An export also embeds the public keys its entries were signed with, in export.getSigningKeys().

docs.title: Deleting ledger entries
docs.text:
Deletion is restricted: the caller must be an administrator and the deployment must set LEDGER_DELETION_ENABLED=true. A chain under an active legal hold cannot be deleted until the hold is released.

// One document's chain.
client.deleteLedgerEntry(documentId);

// Every completed chain older than 90 days.
client.purgeLedger(90);

docs.title: Legal Holds
docs.text:
A legal hold blocks deletion and purging of the evidence it covers until the hold is released. Ledger chains under an active hold cannot be deleted (Philter answers HTTP 423), and neither can the user's entries be purged.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.LegalHoldRequest;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.LegalHoldResponse;
import java.util.List;

LegalHoldRequest request = new LegalHoldRequest();
request.setReference("matter-2026-014");     // your identifier, unique per owner
request.setScopeType("document_chain");      // one document's ledger chain
request.setScopeValue(documentId);           // the document ID
request.setReason("pending litigation");     // optional, recorded with the hold

LegalHoldResponse hold = client.createHold(request);
System.out.println(hold.getSetAt());

reference and scopeType are required, and scopeType must be document_chain or user. A document_chain hold also needs scopeValue, the document ID.

A user hold protects all of its owner's ledger evidence. The owner is the caller, or the user an administrator names with owner, so a user hold needs no scopeValue; one that is given must be the owner's username. Philter returns the owner's username as the hold's scopeValue:

LegalHoldRequest all = new LegalHoldRequest();
all.setReference("matter-2026-015");
all.setScopeType("user");                    // everything the owner holds

LegalHoldResponse mine = client.createHold(all);            // the caller's evidence
LegalHoldResponse theirs = client.createHold(all, "jordan"); // an administrator, for another user
System.out.println(theirs.getScopeValue());                  // "jordan"

Naming another user with owner requires an administrator and ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED; see Owners and Pagination.

Philter rejects with an HTTP 400 a missing reference or scopeType, any other scope type, a document_chain hold without scopeValue, a user hold whose scopeValue names anyone but its owner, and a reference that cannot be used in a request path: one containing /, \, ;, %, or a control character, or that is . or ... Re-using a reference that is already held returns an HTTP 409. Both surface as a ClientException.

// The first page of active holds, most recently set first, and how many there are.
Page<LegalHoldResponse> holds = client.listHolds(null, null);
long total = holds.getTotal();

LegalHoldResponse one = client.getHold("matter-2026-014");

// Release the hold. What it covered becomes deletable again.
client.deleteHold("matter-2026-014");

Since no hold can have a reference that cannot be used in a path, deleteHold always names the hold in the path.

docs.title: Limits and Rules
docs.text:
getLimits() returns the limits and rules Philter enforces, and what the caller may do. Read them instead of hard-coding them, for example to check a name or a password before sending it, so your client stays right when a deployment changes a setting or Philter changes a rule.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.Limits;

Limits limits = client.getLimits();

// Check input before sending it.
if (description.length() > limits.getPolicies().getDescriptionMaxLength()) {
    // Tell the person the description is too long.
}

// Offer only what the caller may do.
boolean canCreateContext = limits.getCaller().getContextCount() < limits.getContexts().getMaxPerUser();
boolean showAllUsers = limits.getCaller().isCrossUserAccess();

Any valid API key can call it, whatever its scopes, including a session key that must first change its password or enroll in MFA. Fields a later Philter adds are ignored.

Group Getters getRequests() getMaxDocumentBytes() for filter and explain, getMaxBodyBytes() for any other request body, getDefaultPageSize(), and getMaxPageSize() for listings. getPassword() getMinCharacters() and getMaxBytes() (in UTF-8). getNames() The rule for custom list names, context names, legal hold references, and usernames: getForbiddenCharacters(), isControlCharactersForbidden(), getReservedNames(), and getRule(), the rule in words. getPolicies() getNameMaxLength(), getNamePattern(), getReservedNamePrefix() (managed_), getReservedNames(), getDefaultPolicyName(), getDescriptionMaxLength(), and getNotesMaxLength(). getCustomLists() getMaxItems(), getItemMaxLength(), and getDescriptionMaxLength(). getRedactLists() getMaxTerms() and getTermMaxLength(), for each of the always-redact and never-redact lists. getContexts() getMaxPerUser(), and getMaxEntries(), beyond which adding an entry evicts the least-read one. getWebhook() getSecretMinLength(). getLegalHolds() getScopeTypes(). getUsers() getRoles() and getReservedUsernames(). getAuditExport() getMaxWindowDays(), getDefaultPageSize(), and getMaxPageSize(). getSessionKeys() getIdleTimeoutMinutes() and getMaxLifetimeMinutes(). getCaller() getRole(), getContextCount(), isCrossUserAccess() (may use owner and all-users listings), and isLedgerDeletion() (may delete and purge ledger chains).

The values are the deployment's: several, such as the request sizes and the session key lifetimes, are settings an administrator can change. For what each means in Philter, see Philter's limits documentation.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
getModels() lists the local PhEye models the deployment has in PHEYE_MODELS_DIRECTORY, ordered by name, and getModel(name) reads one. A policy uses a model by giving its name as a ph-eye filter's phEyeConfiguration.modelPath, and the model then runs inside Philter with no PhEye service. Use the list, for example, to offer only the models a deployment has when building a policy.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.Model;

for (Model model : client.getModels()) {
    System.out.println(model.getName() + " (" + model.getSizeBytes() + " bytes)");
}

Model model = client.getModel("pii-en-xsmall");

Both require Philter 4.0.0 or later and the policies:read scope. The models are the deployment's, the same for every user, and the list is empty when it has none. A key without the scope is a ClientException with status 403, and a name with no model one with status 404.

Getter Value getName() The name a policy gives as modelPath. getEncoder() The encoder the model was trained from, or null when its configuration does not say. getMaxLength() The most words of a text the model reads; later words are not examined. null when its configuration does not say. getMaxWidth() The most words one detected entity can span. null when its configuration does not say. getSizeBytes() The combined size, in bytes, of its gliner_config.json, tokenizer.json, and model.onnx.

Philter does not return a model's location on disk. For how models are deployed and named, see Philter's models documentation.

docs.title: Owners and Pagination
docs.text: Philter scopes its data to the user whose API key made the request. Every call in this client therefore acts on your own policies, contexts, documents, holds, ledger entries, and lists by default.

docs.title: Acting on another user's data
docs.text:
Endpoints that accept an owner have an overload taking that owner's username. It is the last argument everywhere except the listings that take ListOptions, where it comes just before the options, and reidentifyValues(owner, request) and reidentifyText(owner, request), where it comes first.

// Your own policies.
Page<PolicySummary> mine = client.listPolicies(null, null);

// Another user's policies, as an administrator.
Page<PolicySummary> theirs = client.listPolicies("someone@example.com", null);

String policy = client.getPolicy("default", "someone@example.com");

Naming your own username always works. Reaching another user's data requires both an administrator API key and ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED=true on the deployment; without them Philter answers 404, which the client raises as a ClientException. The 404 is deliberate, so an owner name cannot be used to discover which users exist.

Passing null for an owner is the same as omitting it: the call acts on your own data.

getApiKeys is the exception: listing another user's API keys requires an administrator key, but not ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED. Changing and revoking keys take a key ID rather than an owner. See Users and API Keys.

docs.title: Listings: paging, sorting, search, and filters
docs.text:
Every listing returns a page of items and getTotal(), how many items it has across every page, counting only those that match the search and filters. Pass a ListOptions to choose the page, the order, a search, and the listing's filters; every setting is optional, and null options use Philter's defaults: the first 25 items in the listing's default order.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ListOptions;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.Page;

// The third page of 50 policies whose name contains "claims", newest first.
Page<PolicySummary> page = client.listPolicies(null,
        new ListOptions().offset(100).limit(50).sort("created").descending().search("claims"));
long total = page.getTotal();
for (PolicySummary policy : page.getItems()) {
    System.out.println(policy.getName());
}
  • offset(n) and limit(n) choose the page: the limit defaults to 25 and is at most 100.
  • sort(field) orders by one of the listing's fields, below. An unknown field is an HTTP 400 naming the fields it accepts, raised as a ClientException whose getField() is sort.
  • ascending() and descending() set the order. Left out, the default sort keeps its default direction, and any other sort is ascending.
  • search(text) keeps items whose searched field contains the text, ignoring case, matched as plain text. It is sent as q.
  • The filters apply to one listing each: role(...) and active(...) to users, status(...) to documents, and session(...) to API keys.
Method Returns sort (default first) search matches Filters listPolicies(owner, options) Page<PolicySummary> name, created, updated name listPoliciesAcrossUsers(options) Page<PolicySummary> name, created, updated name listManagedPolicies(options) Page<PolicySummary> name name getDeletedPolicies(owner, options) GetDeletedPoliciesResponse name name listPolicyVersions(name, owner, options) Page<PolicyVersionSummary> revision (newest first) listContexts(owner, options) GetContextsResponse name, created name listContextsAcrossUsers(options) GetContextsAcrossUsersResponse name, created name listContextEntries(name, owner, options) GetContextEntriesResponse created (newest first), reads listCustomLists(owner, options) Page<CustomListSummary> name name listCustomListsAcrossUsers(options) Page<CustomListSummary> name name listHolds(owner, options) Page<LegalHoldResponse> set (newest first), reference reference listHoldsAcrossUsers(options) Page<OwnedLegalHoldResponse> set (newest first), reference reference listDocuments(owner, options) GetDocumentsResponse submitted (newest first), fileName status listLedgerChains(owner, options) GetLedgerResponse created (newest first), filename document ID or file name listLedgerChainsAcrossUsers(options) GetLedgerResponse created (newest first), filename document ID or file name getUsers(options) GetUsersResponse username, created username role, active getApiKeys(owner, options) GetApiKeysResponse created (oldest first) session getAuditLog(event, from, to, owner, options) GetAuditLogResponse timestamp (newest first), order only getWebhookDeliveries(owner, options) GetWebhookDeliveriesResponse created (newest first), order only

Items with the same sort value keep a stable order, so paging does not skip or repeat them.

docs.title: Listing across all users
docs.text:
An administrator can list every user's policies, contexts, custom lists, ledger chains, and legal holds in one call, with the ...AcrossUsers(options) methods above. Each item names its owner. The same two conditions apply as for owner: an administrator key and ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED=true, otherwise a 404 raised as a ClientException. Managed policies are not included in listPoliciesAcrossUsers.

Page<PolicySummary> policies = client.listPoliciesAcrossUsers(new ListOptions().search("claims"));
Page<OwnedLegalHoldResponse> holds = client.listHoldsAcrossUsers(new ListOptions().limit(100));

docs.title: Offset and limit overloads
docs.text:
Some listings, such as listContexts(owner, offset, limit) and getUsers(offset, limit), also have an overload that takes offset and limit directly. It returns the same page and total, without sorting or search.

exportAuditLog is paged with offset and limit too, but with its own defaults and a truncation flag; see Audit Log. listRedactLists is not a listing: it returns the two redact lists.

docs.title: Redacting PDF Documents
docs.text:
filter(context, policyName, filename, file) sends a PDF to Philter and returns the redacted result as a ZIP archive (the raw bytes are on the response).

import ai.philterd.philter.model.BinaryFilterResponse;
import java.io.File;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

BinaryFilterResponse response =
        client.filter("my-context", "default", "report.pdf", new File("report.pdf"));

byte[] zip = response.getContent();
Files.write(Path.of("report-redacted.zip"), zip);

Pass filterToPdf(...) instead to receive a redacted PDF rather than a ZIP archive. The arguments are the same.

BinaryFilterResponse response =
        client.filterToPdf("my-context", "default", "report.pdf", new File("report.pdf"));

Files.write(Path.of("report-redacted.pdf"), response.getContent());

docs.title: Redacting a PDF held in memory
docs.text:
Each PDF method also takes the document as a byte[], so a PDF that arrives as an upload can be redacted without first writing an unredacted copy of it to disk. The request is the same as with a File.

// For example, the bytes of an uploaded file.
byte[] pdf = upload.getBytes();

BinaryFilterResponse response = client.filterToPdf("my-context", "default", "upload.pdf", pdf);

String documentId = client.filterAsync("my-context", "default", "upload.pdf", pdf);

docs.title: Submitting a document asynchronously
docs.text:
Both calls above wait for the redaction to finish, which ties up a connection for as long as the document takes. filterAsync(...) and filterToPdfAsync(...) submit the document and return the ID Philter assigned to it. Poll the document's status, then download the result.

String documentId = client.filterAsync("my-context", "default", "report.pdf", new File("report.pdf"));

DocumentStatus status = client.getDocumentState(documentId);
String state = status.getStatus();

byte[] zip = client.getDocument(documentId);            // once the status is COMPLETE

The status is PENDING, PROCESSING, COMPLETE, or FAILED. Downloading a document whose redaction failed returns an HTTP 410, which the client raises as a ClientException; status.getError() says why.

status.getType() says what the job produces, as does getType() on each document from listDocuments(). redaction, a redacted document, is the only type Philter 4.0 returns. It is a string, so a type a later Philter adds is still read.

The status also names the policy the document was submitted with, and so does each document from listDocuments(). Read that revision of the policy to see exactly what redacted it:

String policy = client.getPolicyVersion(status.getPolicyName(), status.getPolicyVersion());

getPolicyVersion() is null only if Philter recorded no policy for the document. A policy's first revision is 0.

To be notified when a redaction finishes instead of polling, set a webhook.

docs.title: Sharing the queue fairly
docs.text:
Philter takes asynchronous documents from different accounts in turns, so one account's large batch does not hold up everyone else. An application that submits for many people under one API key can get the same behavior among those people by passing a fairness key as the last argument to filterAsync(...) or filterToPdfAsync(...), with either a File or a byte[]. Documents queued with different keys take turns.

// For example, an internal user or group ID.
String documentId = client.filterAsync("my-context", "default", "report.pdf", new File("report.pdf"), "group-42");

The key is opaque to Philter and is stored unencrypted with the queued document, so it must not contain personal data such as a name or email address. Use an internal ID instead. A key is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, ., _, : and -; Philter refuses any other value with an HTTP 400. Passing null, or calling the overloads without a key, sends no key; documents queued without a key take turns together, as if they shared one key. The synchronous filter(...) and filterToPdf(...) methods do not take one, since Philter refuses a key on a synchronous request.

Use listDocuments() to list the stored documents and deleteDocument(documentId) to remove one.

docs.title: PII Counts
docs.text:
Philter can record how often each PII type is found, per user's context and UTC day. getPiiCounts reads those counts through Philter's API, so a reporting tool needs an API key rather than a connection to Philter's database. Philter Diffuse uses them for differential-privacy reporting, and they work equally well for any similar purpose, such as a dashboard of PII trends or monitoring how often each type turns up in a context. The counts are counts only: they never carry any PII. These methods need Philter 4.0 or later.

Reading the counts requires an administrator and an API key holding the pii-counts:read scope, since the counts cover the whole deployment. Philter keeps each user's counts apart, and returns another user's context name and username only when its ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED is on; without it, their counts are still returned, unnamed, so totals stay complete. Each call is recorded in the audit log as a pii_counts_retrieved event.

docs.title: Reading the counts
docs.text:
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetPiiCountsResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.PiiCount;
import java.time.LocalDate;

// September 2026 for one context, every page.
GetPiiCountsResponse september = client.getAllPiiCounts(
        LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 1), LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 30), "claims-intake");

if (!september.isRecordingEnabled()) {
    System.out.println("Philter is not recording PII counts now.");
}

for (PiiCount count : september.getCounts()) {
    System.out.println(count.getDay() + " " + count.getOwner() + "/" + count.getContext() + ": " + count.getCounts()
            + " across " + count.getTotalDocuments() + " documents");
}

getAllPiiCounts reads page after page until it has every entry matching the filters. Philter keeps counting while the pages are read, which can shift entries between pages; an entry that comes back twice is returned once, by its id, but for a stable result end the range before the current UTC day. To read one page at a time, use getPiiCounts(from, to, context, owner, offset, limit). Every argument may be null:

  • from and to - the first and last UTC day to return, both inclusive. from after to is an HTTP 400.
  • context - contexts of one name, or null for every context. Without cross-user access, only the caller's own.
  • owner - one user's counts, by username, or null for every user's. Another user's needs cross-user access; otherwise it is an HTTP 404.
  • offset and limit - page through the matches (default 25, at most 100). getTotal() is the number of entries matching the filters.

Entries are returned most recent day first. Each PiiCount has:

  • getId() - identifies this user's context and day, the same on every read: two users' contexts of one name are separate entries.
  • getOwner() - the username whose redactions these are, or null for another user's without cross-user access.
  • getContext() - the context the redactions ran in, or null for another user's without cross-user access.
  • getDay() - the UTC day the redactions ran on.
  • getCounts() - for each PII type, such as SSN, how many redactions that day found at least one of it. A redaction adds at most one to each type, however many of that type it found.
  • getTotalDocuments() - how many redactions that day found any PII. Redactions that found no PII are not counted.
  • getUpdatedAt() - when a redaction was last counted.

docs.title: When recording is off
docs.text: Philter records counts only while the diffuseCountsEnabled admin setting is on, and it is off by default. isRecordingEnabled() says whether Philter is recording now. When it is false, an empty result means nothing is being recorded, not that no PII was found. This is not an error: counts recorded while recording was on are still returned.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• A key without the pii-counts:read scope gets an HTTP 403 with the missing_scope reason.
  • A key whose owner is not an administrator gets an HTTP 403 with the admin_required reason.
  • An invalid date range gets an HTTP 400 with the invalid_request reason.

Each is thrown as a ClientException carrying the reason and Philter's request id. See Error Handling.

For the endpoint itself, see Philter's PII Counts API documentation.

docs.title: Policies: the Redaction Rules
docs.text:
A policy defines which entity types are detected and how each is redacted. Manage them with the policy methods. Policy bodies are JSON strings whose schema is defined by Philter; refer to the Philter API specification for the policy schema.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.Page;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicySummary;
import java.util.List;

// The first page of policies, and how many there are. See Owners and Pagination to sort, search, and page.
Page<PolicySummary> policies = client.listPolicies(null, null);
for (PolicySummary policy : policies.getItems()) {
    System.out.println(policy.getName() + " revision " + policy.getRevision() + ", changed " + policy.getUpdatedAt());
}

// Retrieve a policy's JSON.
String policyJson = client.getPolicy("default");

// Create a policy. The body is the policy JSON. A name already in use is refused.
client.savePolicy("my-policy", policyJson);

// Replace an existing policy with a new revision.
client.replacePolicy("my-policy", policyJson);

// Apply your policy when filtering.
client.filter("my-context", "my-policy", "Some sensitive text...");

// Delete a policy.
client.deletePolicy("my-policy");

savePolicy only creates. A name the owner already uses is refused with a ClientException whose getStatusCode() is 409 and getReason() is policy_exists; replace the policy with replacePolicy instead. replacePolicy is refused with a 404 if there is no such policy, and with a 409 whose reason is policy_changed if the policy changed while the request was writing, or since the read whose entity tag you passed (see Preventing lost updates), in which case read it again and retry. deletePolicy is refused with a 404 if there is no such policy, and with a 409 whose reason is policy_default for the default policy, which cannot be deleted. Both refuse a managed policy with a 409 whose reason is policy_managed.

docs.title: Starting from a template
docs.text:
Rather than keep your own starting policy, which can fall behind the schema as Philter adds filters, start from one of Philter's templates. getPolicyTemplate returns a template's policy JSON, which Philter accepts for its running schema version. Edit it, then save it as a policy:

String template = client.getPolicyTemplate("default");
client.savePolicy("claims", template);

The default template is the one every new user's default policy is created from: it redacts person names, Social Security numbers, and email addresses. Philter detects person names with PhEye, so that part needs a PhEye service your deployment can reach. More templates may be added. A template is not a policy, and cannot be used to redact until it is saved as one. It requires the policies:read scope. A name Philter has no template for is a 404, and the ClientException's getErrorMessage() lists the templates there are.

docs.title: Description and notes
docs.text:
A policy can carry a description (up to 200 characters) and notes (up to 1000). They are not part of the policy's JSON, so getPolicy does not return them and changing them does not create a new revision. Creating and replacing require policies:write, and reading requires policies:read.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicyDetails;

// Create the policy with a description and notes.
client.savePolicy("court", policyJson, "Federal court filings", "Reviewed with the clerk's office.");

// Replacing it without them keeps its current description and notes.
client.replacePolicy("court", policyJson);

// The description, notes, revision, whether it is managed, and when it was created and last updated.
PolicyDetails details = client.getPolicyDetails("court");

// Change them without saving the policy. null leaves a value as it is; "" clears it.
client.setPolicyDetails("court", null, "");

When you pass a description or notes to savePolicy or replacePolicy, the client sends them with the policy in one request, and Philter writes all three together: if the request is refused, for example for notes over 1000 characters, nothing is created or changed. A null value is left out, which keeps the current one; an empty string clears it. With a description or notes, the policy must be a JSON object, or the call throws an IllegalArgumentException before sending anything.

docs.title: Preventing lost updates
docs.text:
Two people, or two clients, editing the same policy could otherwise overwrite each other: each reads the policy, changes it, and saves, and the second save replaces the first without anyone noticing. To prevent that, make your change conditional on what you read:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicyWithETag;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ClientException;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ErrorReasons;

PolicyWithETag read = client.getPolicyWithETag("claims");
String edited = edit(read.getJson());
try {
    // Returns the policy's new entity tag, for the next change.
    String tag = client.replacePolicy("claims", edited, null, null, read.getETag(), null);
} catch (ClientException e) {
    if (ErrorReasons.POLICY_CHANGED.equals(e.getReason())) {
        // Someone else changed the policy: read it again, reapply the edit, and retry.
    } else {
        throw e;
    }
}

An entity tag identifies the policy together with its description and notes, and changes when any of them does; the revision changes only when the policy's content does. Read it with getPolicyWithETag, or from getPolicyDetails(...).getEtag(). Pass it as the expected tag to replacePolicy(name, json, description, notes, expectedETag, owner), setPolicyDetails(name, description, notes, expectedETag, owner), or rollbackPolicy(name, revision, expectedETag, owner). If the policy, its description, or its notes changed since, nothing is written and the call throws a ClientException with status 409 and getReason() ErrorReasons.POLICY_CHANGED. A tag that is not one Philter gave is a 400 whose getField() is If-Match.

Each write returns the new tag, so you can keep editing without reading the policy again: savePolicy and replacePolicy return it, setPolicyDetails and copyPolicy return details whose getEtag() has it, and rollbackPolicy returns it in getETag(). The overloads without an expected tag change the policy whatever its state, as before.

docs.title: Managed policies
docs.text:
Philter ships built-in managed policies, whose names begin with managed_. They can be read and copied, but not changed: replacePolicy, deletePolicy, rollbackPolicy, and setPolicyDetails refuse a managed_ name with a 409 whose getReason() is policy_managed. Copy one with copyPolicy and change the copy instead. Listing them requires policies:read; copying requires policies:write.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicySummary;

// The first page of managed policies, paged like listPolicies and with the same fields.
for (PolicySummary policy : client.listManagedPolicies(null).getItems()) {
    System.out.println(policy.getName() + ": " + policy.getDescription());
}

// Read one by name, as any other policy.
String managedJson = client.getPolicy("managed_common_pii");
PolicyDetails managedDetails = client.getPolicyDetails("managed_common_pii");

// Create a policy of your own from it. The copy is active at once and has its own version history.
PolicyDetails copy = client.copyPolicy("managed_common_pii", "my-pii");

copyPolicy also duplicates one of your own policies. The copy has the source's policy and description; a copy of a managed policy has the note Created from managed policy <name>, and a copy of your own policy keeps its notes. A new name already in use is an HTTP 409, raised as a ClientException whose getReason() is policy_exists.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text:
Philter keeps a revision history for each policy:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicyVersionSummary;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicyRollbackResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.PolicyDiff;

// Newest first, a page at a time; getTotal() counts the retained revisions.
for (PolicyVersionSummary v : client.listPolicyVersions("my-policy", null, null).getItems()) {
    // The author is the username whose change produced the revision, or null when it is not known.
    System.out.println("revision " + v.getRevision() + " @ " + v.getCapturedTimestamp() + " by " + v.getAuthor());
}

String revisionJson = client.getPolicyVersion("my-policy", 2);   // a specific revision
PolicyDiff diff = client.diffPolicy("my-policy", 1, 2);           // diff between revisions
PolicyDiff latest = client.diffPolicy("my-policy");               // the two most recent revisions
for (PolicyDiff.Change change : latest.getChanges()) {
    System.out.println(change.getOp() + " " + change.getPath() + ": " + change.getOldValue() + " -> " + change.getValue());
}

PolicyRollbackResponse rollback = client.rollbackPolicy("my-policy", 1);
System.out.println("rolled back to revision " + rollback.getRevision());
