A rollback is refused with a 404 if the policy or the revision does not exist, and getErrorMessage() says which, for example Revision 99 does not exist. It is refused with a 409 whose getReason() is policy_managed for a managed policy, and policy_changed if the policy changed while the request was writing, or since the read whose entity tag you passed, in which case read it again and retry.

A PolicyDiff has the from and to revisions and the RFC 6902 changes that turn one into the other. Each change has its op (add, remove, or replace), the JSON Pointer path that changed, the new value (null for a removal), and the oldValue before it (null for an addition), both as Gson JsonElements. Without revision numbers, diffPolicy compares the two most recent retained revisions, and from and to say which they were. It reads the retained history, so it works for a deleted policy too. A policy with fewer than two retained revisions, including a name with no history at all, is a 400.

getAuthor() is null for a revision made before Philter recorded authors, for a managed policy, and for a revision first captured when the policy was used to redact.

docs.title: Deleted policies
docs.text:
Deleting a policy keeps its revision history. getDeletedPolicies lists the deleted policies whose history is kept, sorted by name, with each one's latest revision and when and by whom it was deleted. It requires policies:read; an administrator can pass another user's username as owner.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.DeletedPolicy;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetDeletedPoliciesResponse;

GetDeletedPoliciesResponse page = client.getDeletedPolicies(null, 0, 25);
for (DeletedPolicy deleted : page.getPolicies()) {
    System.out.println(deleted.getName() + " revision " + deleted.getLatestRevision()
            + " deleted " + deleted.getDeletedAt() + " by " + deleted.getDeletedBy());
}

getDeletedAt() is an Instant, and it and getDeletedBy() are null for a policy deleted before Philter recorded deletions. getTotal() counts every deleted policy whose history is kept, across pages.

Read a deleted policy's history by its name, as for a live one, with listPolicyVersions and getPolicyVersion. To restore it, save the revision you want under the name with savePolicy; the restored policy continues the same revision numbers. rollbackPolicy only applies to a live policy.

String json = client.getPolicyVersion("claims-2025", 4);
client.savePolicy("claims-2025", json);

docs.title: Compiling PhiSQL
docs.text:
compilePhiSql(phiSql) compiles PhiSQL source into a native policy without saving it. It requires the policies:read scope.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.CompilePolicyResponse;

CompilePolicyResponse compiled = client.compilePhiSql("POLICY ssn_only;\nREDACT SSN WITH MASK;");
client.savePolicy(compiled.getName(), compiled.getPolicyJson());

The result carries the compiled policy (getPolicy() as a JSON object, getPolicyJson() as a string for savePolicy), the getName() from the source's POLICY declaration (null when it has none), and the getDescription() when the source declares one. The policy is validated before it is returned. Supply a name to savePolicy if the source had none.

Source that fails to parse or compile, or a compiled policy that fails validation, is rejected with an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException carrying the compiler's message.

docs.title: Users and API Keys
docs.text:
Users own API keys and the policies, contexts, and other resources made with them. Automation authenticates with long-lived API keys; a person can also sign in with a password through a user interface, which gets a session key (see Sign-in, Passwords, and MFA). These calls create and manage users and their keys, for example to stand up a deployment in CI, in a marketplace image, or for a test harness.

Every user call on this page requires an administrator's key, except getCurrentUser, along with the scope noted for each. A user can manage its own API keys without an administrator; managing another user's requires one. Philter refuses both a missing scope and a non-administrator with an HTTP 403, raised as a ClientException. The message tells them apart: a missing scope names the scope (This API key does not have the 'users:read' scope.), and a non-administrator is told an administrator is required (Listing users requires an administrator.).

docs.title: Creating a user
docs.text:
Requires the users:write scope.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.CreatedUserResponse;

CreatedUserResponse user = client.createUser("ci", "ci@example.com");

System.out.println(user.getId());        // 6aa5792a403075186a843960
System.out.println(user.getUsername());  // ci
System.out.println(user.getRole());      // user

// An administrator.
CreatedUserResponse admin = client.createUser("ops", null, "admin");

A user's id, from getId() here and on every User (including getCurrentUser()), is a 24-character hex string. Audit events refer to the user by it, in AuditEvent.getApiKeyId(). The email is optional. The role is user or admin, and defaults to user. createUser(username, email, role, password) also gives the user a password, which they must change at next sign-in; without one, the user can only use API keys. See Passwords. The new user gets a default policy and context.

An email address must have one @, something on each side, a dot in the domain, and no whitespace, and be at most 254 characters. A missing or reserved username (me), any other role, or an email address that does not follow that rule is rejected with an HTTP 400. A username already taken, by an active user or a deactivated one holding the name in reserve, returns an HTTP 409. Both surface as a ClientException carrying Philter's explanation.

docs.title: Reading users
docs.text:
Requires the users:read scope.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.CurrentUser;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetUsersResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.User;

// Users sorted by username, including deactivated users. Paged with offset and limit.
GetUsersResponse page = client.getUsers(0, 100);
long total = page.getTotal();
for (User u : page.getUsers()) {
    System.out.println(u.getUsername() + " " + u.getRole() + " " + u.isActive());
}

User ci = client.getUser("ci");

// The user that owns the calling key, with the deployment's MFA settings. Does not require an administrator.
CurrentUser me = client.getCurrentUser();
boolean offerMfa = me.isMfaAvailable() && !me.isMfaEnabled();

getUsers defaults to the first 25 users and returns at most 100 per page. getUser returns an HTTP 404 for a username that does not exist.

docs.title: Changing a user
docs.text:
Requires the users:write scope. Each call returns the updated User.

client.setUserRole("ci", "admin");

// Set or change the email address; null, an empty string, or only spaces removes it.
client.setUserEmail("ci", "platform-team@example.com");
client.setUserEmail("ci", null);

// Its API keys stop working; the user and its data are kept.
client.deactivateUser("ci");

// Its API keys work again.
client.reactivateUser("ci");

The email address follows the same rule as when creating a user, after Philter trims surrounding whitespace; one that does not is an HTTP 400 carrying Philter's message. It is not how a user is addressed or signs in, so changing it changes nothing else. Philter records the change as a user_email_changed audit event, without the address; see Auditing.

A deactivated user keeps its username in reserve, so it cannot be recreated. Philter refuses, with an HTTP 409, demoting or deactivating the last active administrator, deactivating your own user, deactivating a user that is already deactivated, and reactivating one that is already active. An unknown username is an HTTP 404.

docs.title: Listing API keys
docs.text:
Requires the api-keys:read scope.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ApiKey;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetApiKeysResponse;

// The calling key's user's active keys, oldest first. Paged with offset and limit.
GetApiKeysResponse mine = client.getApiKeys();
for (ApiKey k : mine.getApiKeys()) {
    System.out.println(k.getId() + " " + k.getPrefix() + " " + k.getScopes() + " " + k.isBootstrap());
}

// Another user's keys. Requires an administrator.
GetApiKeysResponse theirs = client.getApiKeys("ci", 0, 100);

// Only long-lived keys, leaving out session keys: false. Only session keys: true.
GetApiKeysResponse longLived = client.getApiKeys(null, 0, 100, false);

Each key has its ID, a prefix to tell keys apart, its scopes, when it was created, and whether it is the bootstrap key seeded from PHILTER_BOOTSTRAP_API_KEY. Session keys, issued when a person signs in, are listed too, with their expiry; see Session keys. The key itself is never returned after it is created. Listing another user's keys requires an administrator, but not ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED; an unknown username is an HTTP 404.

docs.title: Creating an API key
docs.text:
List the scopes a key can carry before choosing them, rather than hard-coding the names. Any valid key can list them, whatever its scopes, and the list includes any scope Philter adds later.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ApiKeyScopeDescription;

for (ApiKeyScopeDescription scope : client.listApiKeyScopes().getScopes()) {
    System.out.println(scope.getName() + ": " + scope.getDescription());
}
// redact: Redact text and documents, and explain redactions.
// contexts:read: List and read contexts and their entries, including exports.
// ...

Creating a key requires the api-keys:write scope.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.CreatedApiKeyResponse;
import java.util.List;

// A key for the calling key's own user. Does not require an administrator.
CreatedApiKeyResponse mine = client.createApiKey(List.of("redact"));

// A key for another user. Requires an administrator.
CreatedApiKeyResponse key = client.createApiKey("ci", List.of("redact", "policies:read"));

System.out.println(key.getApiKey());  // the only time this value is available
System.out.println(key.getId());      // used to change its scopes or revoke it

Capture the value from the response. Philter stores only the key's hash, so a value not read here cannot be recovered; the only remedy is to create another key.

At least one scope is required, and each must name a scope Philter defines. An unrecognized name is refused with an HTTP 400 rather than dropped, so a key is never silently narrower than the one that was asked for. The requested scopes must also be a subset of those the calling key holds: a key cannot grant a scope it does not itself carry, and trying returns an HTTP 403.

For another user, an HTTP 404 means there is no active user with that username. A deactivated account counts as absent, though its username stays reserved and cannot be recreated. Philter checks the scopes before it resolves the user, so a caller who could not grant those scopes anyway learns nothing about whether the username exists.

docs.title: Changing a key's scopes and revoking a key
docs.text:
Requires the api-keys:write scope. Both take the key's ID. A user can change or revoke its own keys; an administrator can change or revoke any user's.

// Replace the key's scopes. The key value does not change.
ApiKey changed = client.setApiKeyScopes(keyId, List.of("redact"));

// Revoke the key. It cannot be restored.
client.revokeApiKey(keyId);

The calling key cannot change or revoke a key holding a scope it does not hold (HTTP 403), and cannot change its own scopes, even to narrow them, or revoke itself (HTTP 409); use another key. A key the caller may not manage, including another user's key for a non-administrator, is an HTTP 404.

To rotate a key, create its replacement with createApiKey(scopes), switch the integration to the new key, then revoke the old key using the new one.

Philter caches each resolved key for up to API_KEY_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS (60 by default). Revoking a key or changing its scopes takes effect at once on the Philter instance that handles the request and on every instance sharing its Valkey or Redis cache. Other nodes in a cluster that do not share the cache may accept the old key or scopes until their cache entry expires.

docs.title: Auditing
docs.text: Every change on this page is recorded in Philter's audit log. Creating a user, setting a role, setting an email address, deactivating, and reactivating record user_created, user_role_changed, user_email_changed, user_deactivated, and user_reactivated events naming the calling administrator as the principal, with the calling API key in the details. An api_key_created event names the new key as the principal and the user it belongs to as the object, as a key made in the dashboard does; the caller who asked for it is in the event's details, along with the scopes granted. Changing a key's scopes records api_key_scopes_changed with the scopes before and after, and revoking one records api_key_deleted.

docs.title: Re-identifying Redacted Values
docs.text:
Values redacted with one of Philter's reversible strategies can be re-identified one value at a time. Philter accepts two strategies, named exactly as the policy names them:

Strategy Notes CRYPTO_REPLACE Requires policyName, which names the policy whose key was used. FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE policyName is not required.

The ReidentifyStrategy enum names both. setStrategy(String) is still available for sending a strategy name the enum does not have.

A reason is required on every request; Philter records it in the audit log.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ReidentifyRequest;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ReidentifyResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ReidentifyStrategy;
import java.util.List;

ReidentifyRequest request = new ReidentifyRequest();
request.setStrategy(ReidentifyStrategy.CRYPTO_REPLACE);
request.setPolicyName("my-policy");
request.setReason("authorized support investigation");
request.setValues(List.of("<redacted-value>"));

ReidentifyResponse response = client.reidentifyValues(request);
for (ReidentifyResponse.ReidentifyResult result : response.getResults()) {
    // The original value, or null with an error saying why it could not be re-identified.
    System.out.println(result.getEncrypted() + " -> " + result.getDecrypted() + " " + result.getError());
}

// An administrator re-identifying another user's values passes the owner first.
client.reidentifyValues("someone@example.com", request);

There is one result for each value, in the order sent. A value that cannot be re-identified does not fail the request: its result has an error and no decrypted value.

Any other strategy name, a missing reason, or an empty value list is rejected with an HTTP 400, which the client raises as a ClientException.

reidentifyValues is per value: pass the redacted values you want restored. To restore a whole text, see Re-identifying a text. Neither applies to non-reversible strategies such as redaction, masking, or hashing.

docs.title: Re-identifying a text
docs.text:
reidentifyText takes a text, such as a redacted document or an LLM's response to a redacted prompt, and returns it with each CRYPTO_REPLACE value restored. Philter finds every {{...}} token in the text, decrypts it with the named policy's key, and puts the original value in its place. text, policyName, and reason are all required.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ReidentifyTextRequest;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.ReidentifyTextResponse;

ReidentifyTextRequest request = new ReidentifyTextRequest();
request.setText(redactedText);
request.setPolicyName("my-policy");
request.setReason("authorized claims review");

ReidentifyTextResponse response = client.reidentifyText(request);
String original = response.getText();
System.out.println(response.getFound() + " found, " + response.getRestored() + " restored, "
        + response.getFailed() + " failed");

// An administrator restoring a text redacted under another user's policy passes the owner first.
client.reidentifyText("someone@example.com", request);

Limits:

  • Only CRYPTO_REPLACE tokens are restored. FPE_ENCRYPT_REPLACE replacements cannot be told apart from ordinary data in a text, so reverse them with reidentifyValues.
  • A token that does not decrypt is left in the text unchanged and counted in getFailed(). This includes a token encrypted under another policy's key and one altered after redaction, for example shortened by an LLM. The call still succeeds.
  • A token altered so that it is no longer {{ followed by Base64 and }}, for example split by a space or missing a brace, is not found, so it is counted in neither getFound() nor getFailed() and is left unchanged. A model's response can therefore come back partly restored with getFailed() at 0: check the text, not only the counts.

A missing field or a policy without a crypto key is an HTTP 400, a key without the reidentify scope a 403, and a policy that does not exist a 404, each raised as a ClientException. The owner overload behaves as it does for reidentifyValues: another user's policy requires an administrator and ADMIN_CROSS_USER_ACCESS_ENABLED=true, and is otherwise a 404. A text larger than the deployment's request body limit, getLimits().getRequests().getMaxBodyBytes() (256 KiB by default), is a 413. Requires Philter 4.0.0 or later.

docs.title: Always-Redact and Never-Redact Lists
docs.text:
Each account has two term lists that apply across its policies: terms to always redact, and terms to never redact.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.RedactLists;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.RedactListsRequest;

// Read both lists.
RedactLists lists = client.listRedactLists();
List<String> always = lists.getAlwaysRedact();
List<String> never = lists.getNeverRedact();

// Replace both lists in full. This is not a merge: a list you leave null or empty is cleared.
client.createRedactList(new RedactListsRequest(List.of("Project X"), List.of("Acme")));

// Append to the existing lists instead of replacing them. A null list is left as it is.
client.updateRedactList(new RedactListsRequest(List.of("Project Y"), null));

A list holds up to 1000 terms of up to 100 characters each; exceeding either is an HTTP 400, raised as a ClientException.

docs.title: One list at a time, without losing changes
docs.text:
getRedactList reads one list with its revision, and replaceRedactList replaces only that list, leaving the other as it is. Every write of a list moves its revision forward; a list never written is at 0. listRedactLists() also gives both revisions, as getAlwaysRedactRevision() and getNeverRedactRevision().

Pass the revision you read to replaceRedactList, and the list is replaced only if nobody changed it in between. Otherwise nothing is written and Philter answers HTTP 409, raised as a ClientException whose getReason() is ErrorReasons.REDACT_LIST_CHANGED. Read the list again, apply your change to what you read, and retry:

import ai.philterd.philter.model.RedactList;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.RedactListTerms;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ClientException;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.exceptions.ErrorReasons;

boolean written = false;
for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 3 && !written; attempt++) {
    RedactListTerms current = client.getRedactList(RedactList.ALWAYS);
    // The whole list is replaced, so start from the terms it has.
    List<String> terms = new ArrayList<>(current.getTerms());
    terms.add("Project X");
    try {
        client.replaceRedactList(RedactList.ALWAYS, terms, current.getRevision());
        written = true;
    } catch (ClientException e) {
        if (!ErrorReasons.REDACT_LIST_CHANGED.equals(e.getReason())) {
            throw e;
        }
        // Someone else changed the list; read it again and reapply the change.
    }
}
if (!written) {
    // The list kept changing; tell the person their change was not saved.
}

With a null revision, replaceRedactList replaces the list whatever its revision. A null or empty terms list clears it. The result is the list as written, with its new revision, ready for the next change. Philter trims terms and drops blank ones. Reading requires lists:read and replacing lists:write, and both take an owner for an administrator acting on another user's lists. createRedactList and updateRedactList, which write both lists at once, take no revision.

These lists are distinct from the named custom lists, which a policy references by name.

docs.title: Redacting Text
docs.text:
filter(context, policyName, text) sends text to Philter and returns the redacted text. This is the core redaction call.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.FilterResponse;

FilterResponse response = client.filter("my-context", "default",
        "His name is George Washington and his SSN is 123-45-6789.");

String redacted = response.getFilteredText();
// e.g. "His name is {{{REDACTED-person}}} and his SSN is {{{REDACTED-ssn}}}."
// (the exact replacement depends on the policy's filter strategies)

String documentId = response.getDocumentId();  // assigned by Philter
String context = response.getContext();         // echoes "my-context"

Pass a filename with the four-argument overload to record the source of the text against the document:

FilterResponse response = client.filter("my-context", "default", "notes.txt", text);

explain(context, policyName, filename, text) takes a filename the same way.

The replacement text (redaction tokens, masking characters, encrypted values, and so on) is entirely determined by the policy you name. See Policies.

docs.title: Signed responses
docs.text:
Philter can sign the text it returns, so a recipient can verify that the response came from a specific deployment, was governed by the named policy, and was not modified. Pass true as the last argument of filter or explain to ask for a signature:

FilterResponse response = client.filter("my-context", "default", null, text, true);

String signature = response.getSignature();  // a compact ES256 JWT, or null if unsigned

A deployment with output signing enabled (the signingEnabled admin setting) signs every filter and explain response whether or not you ask, and passing false does not turn that off. PDF responses are not signed.

The client does not verify signatures. To verify one, fetch the public key named by the JWT's kid with getSigningKeyDetails(keyId), which needs no API key, check the ES256 signature, and check that the bodyHash claim is the SHA-256 of the response body. For filter the body is getFilteredText(); for explain it is getResponseBody(), the JSON exactly as Philter sent it.

import com.google.gson.JsonObject;
import com.google.gson.JsonParser;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.KeyFactory;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.security.PublicKey;
import java.security.Signature;
import java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec;
import java.util.Base64;

String[] parts = signature.split("\\.");
Base64.Decoder base64url = Base64.getUrlDecoder();

// The public key named by the JWT's kid.
JsonObject header = JsonParser.parseString(new String(base64url.decode(parts[0]), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)).getAsJsonObject();
String pem = client.getSigningKeyDetails(header.get("kid").getAsString()).getPem()
        .replace("-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----", "").replace("-----END PUBLIC KEY-----", "").replaceAll("\\s", "");
PublicKey publicKey = KeyFactory.getInstance("EC").generatePublic(new X509EncodedKeySpec(Base64.getDecoder().decode(pem)));

// The ES256 signature over the JWT's header and payload.
Signature verifier = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format");
verifier.initVerify(publicKey);
verifier.update((parts[0] + "." + parts[1]).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
boolean signatureValid = verifier.verify(base64url.decode(parts[2]));

// The body the signature covers.
JsonObject payload = JsonParser.parseString(new String(base64url.decode(parts[1]), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)).getAsJsonObject();
byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(response.getFilteredText().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
StringBuilder bodyHash = new StringBuilder();
for (byte b : digest) {
    bodyHash.append(String.format("%02x", b));
}
boolean bodyMatches = bodyHash.toString().equals(payload.get("bodyHash").getAsString());

The payload also carries policyName, policyVersion, documentId, and iat, the time it was signed. Cache public keys by ID: after the key is rotated, older signatures still verify against the key they name. See Philter's Output Signing documentation.

docs.title: Sign-in, Passwords, and MFA
docs.text:
A user interface can sign a person in as their own Philter user, without holding an administrator key of its own. The interface sends the person's username and password, and Philter returns a short-lived session key for that user, which the interface uses for the person's requests. Philter stays the user store, the user's role and the key's scopes decide access, and the audit log names the person.

Password sign-in is disabled unless the deployment sets PASSWORD_SIGN_IN_ENABLED=true. While it is disabled, the sign-in calls fail with an HTTP 404, raised as a ClientException. A user can only sign in once they have a password; see Passwords.

docs.title: Sign-in options
docs.text:
Before anyone signs in, a sign-in page can read the rules a new password must meet with getSignInOptions(). It sends no API key, even when the client has one.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.SignInOptions;
import java.util.Optional;

Optional<SignInOptions> options = client.getSignInOptions();
if (options.isPresent()) {
    int minimum = options.get().getPassword().getMinCharacters();   // 16
    int maximumBytes = options.get().getPassword().getMaxBytes();    // 72, in UTF-8
} else {
    // Password sign-in is not enabled on this deployment: hide the sign-in form.
}

When password sign-in is not enabled (PASSWORD_SIGN_IN_ENABLED is off), Philter answers HTTP 404, as for its other sign-in endpoints, and getSignInOptions() returns an empty Optional rather than throwing. A Philter older than philterd/philter#159, which has no such endpoint, answers 404 too, so it also reads as password sign-in being off. Any other failure is thrown as usual. A signed-in client reads the same rules, with the rest of Philter's limits, from getLimits().

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
signIn needs no API key. Its result is either a session key or, for a user enrolled in MFA, a challenge.

import ai.philterd.philter.PhilterClient;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.SignInResponse;

SignInResponse result = client.signIn("jordan", password);

if (result.isMfaRequired()) {
    // Ask the person for a code from their authenticator app. The challenge expires in five minutes.
    result = client.completeSignIn(result.getChallenge(), code);
}

// A client for the person's own requests, using the session key.
PhilterClient session = new PhilterClient.PhilterClientBuilder()
        .withEndpoint("https://localhost:8080")
        .withApiKey("Bearer " + result.getApiKey())
        .build();

The session key holds every scope, with the user's role still deciding administrator access. It cannot create API keys. It expires after a period without a request (getIdleExpiresAt(), moved forward by each request) or at the end of its maximum lifetime (getExpiresAt()). A request with an expired or revoked key is refused with an UnauthorizedException, which a user interface should treat as the session having ended.

Two flags restrict what the key can do:

  • isPasswordChangeRequired() - an administrator set the password, so the key can only change it with changePassword and sign out. Changing it revokes the key, and the person signs in again with the new password.
  • isMfaEnrollmentRequired() - the deployment requires MFA and the user is not enrolled, so the key can only enroll and sign out. Confirming enrollment revokes the key, and the person signs in again, with a code.

Any other request with a restricted key is refused with an HTTP 403, raised as a ClientException that says what to do first.

To sign out, call signOut() on the client holding the session key. It revokes that key. A long-lived key cannot revoke itself, so signOut() with one is an HTTP 409.

session.signOut();

docs.title: Failed sign-ins
Signing in on behalf of a person
docs.text:
Philter rate-limits sign-ins by client address (SIGN_IN_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE) and records that address on sign_in_succeeded and sign_in_failed audit events. When an application signs people in through one client, every sign-in comes from the application's address, so its users share one rate-limit budget and the audit log cannot tell them apart. Pass each person's address instead:

// The address of the person's connection to the application. If the application is itself behind a
// load balancer, use the client address it resolves from that balancer's header, not the balancer's.
String personAddress = httpRequest.getRemoteAddr();

// The person's browser, from their request to the application.
String personUserAgent = httpRequest.getHeader("User-Agent");

SignInResponse result = client.signIn(username, password, personAddress, personUserAgent);
if (result.isMfaRequired()) {
    result = client.completeSignIn(result.getChallenge(), code, personAddress, personUserAgent);
}

The address is sent as X-Forwarded-For. Philter uses it only when the request comes from an address in its TRUSTED_PROXIES, which by default is loopback only, so unless the application runs on the same host as Philter, list the application's address there; otherwise, and for a value that is not an IP address, it uses the address of the connection. A port is allowed and ignored. Pass an address the application determined itself, not one the person's browser supplied, such as their own X-Forwarded-For, which they can set to anything. A null or empty address, or one of only spaces, sends the client's withClientAddress value instead, or no header without one; a given address is sent instead of that value. Surrounding spaces are trimmed, and an address containing a comma, a control character such as a line break, a character outside ASCII, or a space within it is refused with an IllegalArgumentException before anything is sent.

Philter also records the user agent of the request that issues a session key, so a person can tell their sessions apart. Without the person's user agent, every session the application signs in shows the application's own client (Java-http-client/...). The four-argument signIn and completeSignIn send the given user agent as the sign-in request's User-Agent. Pass it on both calls of an MFA sign-in, since the key is issued by the second. A null or empty user agent, or one of only spaces, sends the client's own, as the shorter overloads do. Surrounding spaces are trimmed, and characters outside printable ASCII, such as line breaks, are left out, so a user agent cannot add a header. Philter keeps at most 256 characters of it and does not check it, so it describes the device rather than proving anything about it. Only the sign-in requests send it; later requests with the session key send the client's own.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
A password is 16 characters to 72 bytes in UTF-8. Setting, changing, or resetting a password revokes the user's session keys; long-lived API keys are not affected.

// A person changes their own password. Requires users:write; not an administrator.
client.changePassword(currentPassword, newPassword);

// An administrator sets or resets another user's password. The user must change it at next sign-in.
client.setPassword("jordan", temporaryPassword);

// An administrator creates a user with a password, which the user must change at next sign-in.
client.createUser("jordan", "jordan@example.com", "user", temporaryPassword);

changePassword needs the current password, so a stolen key cannot replace its own user's password unnoticed. A wrong current password is an HTTP 403, and a user without a password, whose first password an administrator sets, is an HTTP 409.

setPassword on the calling administrator's own user sets only the first password, with no change required. This is how the admin user gets a password: call it with the bootstrap API key. After that, the administrator changes it with changePassword.

User.isPasswordSet() and User.isPasswordChangeRequired() report a user's password state; the password and its hash are never returned.

docs.title: Multi-factor authentication
docs.text:
A user who signs in with a password can add TOTP multi-factor authentication, with an authenticator app. MFA is available only when an administrator turns on mfaAvailable in the admin settings; mfaRequired makes every user who signs in enroll. Enrolling and removing your own enrollment require users:write but not an administrator. A user who is not an administrator cannot read the admin settings, so getCurrentUser() returns isMfaAvailable() and isMfaRequired() for deciding whether to offer enrollment.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.MfaEnrollment;

// Start, with the person's current password: show the URI as a QR code, or have the person type in the
// secret. Neither is returned again. A wrong password counts toward the sign-in lockout.
MfaEnrollment enrollment = client.startMfaEnrollment(currentPassword);
String qrCodeContent = enrollment.getOtpauthUri();

// Confirm with a code from the app. This revokes the user's session keys.
client.confirmMfaEnrollment(code);

// Remove your own enrollment. It takes a valid code, so a stolen key cannot turn MFA off.
client.removeMfaEnrollment(code);

After five consecutive bad codes the user's MFA is locked. An administrator unlocks it, or removes the enrollment for a person who has lost their device:

client.unlockUserMfa("jordan");
client.removeUserMfa("jordan");

User.isMfaEnabled() and User.isMfaLocked() report a user's MFA state; the secret is never returned.

docs.title: Session keys
docs.text:
getApiKeys lists session keys alongside long-lived keys. ApiKey.isSession() marks them, and getExpiresAt(), getIdleExpiresAt(), and getLastUsedAt() give their expiry and last use; they are null for long-lived keys. Revoke one with revokeApiKey, or every session key a user holds, signing the person out everywhere, with revokeSessionKeys, which requires an administrator:

int revoked = client.revokeSessionKeys("jordan");

Pass session to getApiKeys to list only one kind of key; the total then counts only those.

docs.title: Your sessions
docs.text:
A person can see where they are signed in and sign out the sessions they do not recognize. Each session key carries the client that signed in: getClientAddress() and getUserAgent() (such as a browser, at most 256 characters). For sessions an application signs in on a person's behalf, these are the address and user agent it passed; see Signing in on behalf of a person. isCurrent() is true for the key making the request, so a user interface can mark the session it is using. Philter keeps the address and user agent only while the session lasts, and they are null for long-lived keys.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.ApiKey;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetApiKeysResponse;

// With the client built from the sign-in result above. true lists only session keys, false only
// long-lived keys, and null both.
GetApiKeysResponse sessions = session.getApiKeys(null, null, null, true);
for (ApiKey key : sessions.getApiKeys()) {
    System.out.println(key.getUserAgent() + " from " + key.getClientAddress() + ", last used "
            + key.getLastUsedAt() + (key.isCurrent() ? " (this session)" : ""));
}

// Sign out everywhere else, and stay signed in here.
long revoked = session.signOutOtherSessions();

signOutOtherSessions() revokes every session key your user holds except the one making the request. Called with a long-lived key, it revokes all of the user's session keys. Long-lived keys are never affected. It requires api-keys:write but not an administrator, because it only ends your own sessions. To end one session, revoke its key with revokeApiKey.

SignInResponse.getId() is also the session key's ID as the listing gives it, another way to recognize the current session.

setApiKeyScopes and revokeApiKey refuse the key making the request with an HTTP 409, so a session key cannot change its own scopes; it ends itself with signOut().

Session keys are checked against the database on every request, so a revoked or expired session key is refused on every Philter instance at once.

docs.title: Webhook
docs.text:
When an asynchronous PDF redaction completes or fails, Philter can notify your application with a signed HTTP POST, instead of you polling the document's status. Each user has at most one webhook: a URL and a shared secret Philter signs each request body with. Synchronous redactions never produce a webhook.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.Webhook;

Webhook webhook = client.setWebhook("https://hooks.example.com/philter",
        "a-shared-secret-of-at-least-16-characters");

// The URL, and whether a secret is set. The secret is never returned.
Webhook current = client.getWebhook();
String url = current.getUrl();           // null when no webhook is set
boolean hasSecret = current.isSecretSet();

// Change the URL and keep the secret already set.
client.setWebhook("https://hooks.example.com/philter/v2", null);

// Stop delivery. Succeeds when no webhook is set.
client.removeWebhook();

getWebhook and getWebhookDeliveries require the webhooks:read scope; setWebhook, testWebhook, and removeWebhook require webhooks:write. None requires an administrator for your own webhook.

setWebhook sets the URL and the secret. With a null secret it sends none, and Philter keeps the secret already set, so the URL can change without rotating the secret. Philter refuses, with an HTTP 400 raised as a ClientException carrying its reason, and saves nothing for:

  • a missing URL, or a missing secret when none is set yet;
  • a URL that is not http or https;
  • a host the administrator's webhook destination allowlist (see Admin Settings) does not permit, or, with no allowlist, a private or loopback address;
  • a secret shorter than 16 characters.

Setting, testing, and removing a webhook are recorded in Philter's audit log as webhook_configured, webhook_tested, and webhook_removed. The URL and secret are not recorded.

docs.title: Testing a webhook
docs.text:
testWebhook sends one signed WEBHOOK_TEST event to the webhook now, so you can check the receiver's URL and its signature check without redacting a document. It is signed and checked against the destination allowlist as a real delivery is. The test is sent once, without retries, and is not added to the delivery history.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.WebhookTestResult;

WebhookTestResult result = client.testWebhook();
if (result.isDelivered()) {
    System.out.println("Delivered in " + result.getDurationMillis() + " ms");
} else {
    // The receiver's status, or null when it could not be reached, and why.
    System.out.println(result.getStatusCode() + ": " + result.getError());
}

A receiver that refuses the test, or cannot be reached, is a result with isDelivered() false, not an exception. getDeliveryId() is the test's X-Philter-Delivery-Id, to find it in the receiver's logs. With no webhook set, Philter answers with an HTTP 409 whose getReason() is webhook_not_set, raised as a ClientException.

Philter waits for the receiver up to its webhook connect and response timeouts (5 and 10 seconds by default) before answering. A client built with withTimeout shorter than their sum can end the call with an IOException instead of a result.

docs.title: Delivery history
docs.text:
getWebhookDeliveries lists the events Philter queued for your webhook, newest first, with how sending each one went. Use it to find out why a receiver did not get an event.

import ai.philterd.philter.model.GetWebhookDeliveriesResponse;
import ai.philterd.philter.model.WebhookDelivery;

GetWebhookDeliveriesResponse page = client.getWebhookDeliveries(null, 0, 25);
for (WebhookDelivery delivery : page.getDeliveries()) {
    System.out.println(delivery.getEvent() + " for " + delivery.getDocumentId() + ": " + delivery.getStatus()
            + " after " + delivery.getAttempts() + " attempts" + (delivery.getLastError() == null ? ""
            : " (" + delivery.getLastError() + ")"));
}

A delivery's status is WebhookDelivery.PENDING (waiting for its next attempt, at getNextAttemptAt()), PROCESSING (being sent), DELIVERED, or FAILED (every attempt failed, and Philter stopped trying). Its times are Instants: getCreatedAt(), getUpdatedAt(), getNextAttemptAt(), and getDeliveredAt(), the last two null when they do not apply. getTotal() counts every delivery. limit defaults to 25 and is at most 100.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: WebhookEvents names the events Philter sends, in the body's event field and the X-Philter-Event header: DOCUMENT_REDACTION_COMPLETE, DOCUMENT_REDACTION_FAILED, and WEBHOOK_TEST, which only testWebhook sends. A receiver should accept a test with a 2xx status and otherwise ignore it. For the request bodies and how to verify their signatures, see Philter's webhook documentation.

docs.title: Another user's webhook
docs.text:
Each call has an overload taking an owner username as its last argument, for an administrator to act on another user's webhook. See Owners and Pagination for the conditions.

Webhook theirs = client.getWebhook("someone@example.com");
client.setWebhook(url, secret, "someone@example.com");
client.testWebhook("someone@example.com");
client.getWebhookDeliveries("someone@example.com", 0, 25);
client.removeWebhook("someone@example.com");
